headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: DJT, TSLA, CRWV, NVO Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out the companies making the biggest moves in premarket trading: Trump Media & Technology Group — Shares of President Donald Trump 's social media company and tech company were down 11% after a decisive victory by Democrats in the U.S. midterm elections Tuesday night. Trump owns 41% of the company, which owns social media platform Truth Social. Democrats taking control of Congress add a check on the president's policies. Tesla , SpaceX — Shares of Elon Musk's Tesla and SpaceX dropped nearly 6% and more than 7%, respectively. The moves come after the Democrats won control of the House of Representatives and the Senate. Many of the newly elected candidates have critical positions on the rapid data center build-out that's been fueled by artificial intelligence. SpaceX operates an AI supercomputing infrastructure in Tennessee and Mississippi , while Tesla has one in Texas. Neocloud stocks — Shares of so-called neocloud companies moved lower, with CoreWeave dropping 7%, Iren tumbling 6% and Nebius slipping about 5%. The Democratic wins in Texas and rejection of data centers in ballots across the country is expected to create hurdles for data center plays. Novo Nordisk — Shares gained over 6% after the global healthcare company reported earnings of 5.79 Danish kroner, or about 63 cents per share, compared with Wall Street expectations of 5.10 kroner, or about 55 cents. The company raised its fiscal 2026 outlook, citing expectations for GLP-1 product sales. CVS Health — Shares fell more than 2% after the company said it would split into two separate publicly traded companies by the first half of 2028. The move would reverse CVS' $78 billion acquisition of Aetna and separate the company's retail pharmacy business. McDonald's — The fast-food restaurant chain reported mixed quarterly results , sending shares 2% higher. Adjusted earnings came in at $3.57 per share, topping the $3.38 expected from analysts polled by LSEG. However, its revenue of $7.16 billion fell short of the $7.29 billion consensus estimate. Duolingo — The language learning software company surged 18% after reporting third-quarter revenue of $309 million. That topped an LSEG consensus of $303 million. Monthly active users totaled 153 million for the quarter, exceeding a 149 million forecast. Adjusted EBITDA margin also topped expectations. Alight — The employee benefits consultancy popped 22% after raising its outlook for the full-year 2026. Alight sees revenue in a range of $2.115 billion to $2.125 billion, versus the FactSet consensus estimate of $2.09 billion. Adjusted EBITDA guidance of $410 million to $420 million also beat the Street's estimates of $404.4 million. Avis Budget Group — The car rental agency slid about 2% on mixed third-quarter results. Avis earned $5.15 a share, a steep decline from $10.11 per share in the year-earlier period. Revenue clocked in at $3.44 billion, slightly ahead of a FactSet consensus of $3.42 billion. Advanced Micro Devices — The chipmaker was last little changed after reporting stronger-than-expected third-quarter earnings . Adjusted earnings of $2.09 per share topped estimates for $1.95, according to analysts polled by LSEG. Revenue forecasts for the current quarter also came in above estimates. Toast — The restaurant management software company dropped 5% despite delivering third-quarter results that topped estimates, according to FactSet. Toast also said CFO Elena Gomez will leave the company at the end of 2026 and will be replaced by senior vice president of finance Michael Senno. Skyworks Solutions — The provider of wireless networking services slumped about 11% after guidance for the current quarter disappointed the Street. Skyworks anticipates adjusted earnings of about $1.25 per share and revenue of $1.80 billion to $1.90 billion in the fiscal first quarter, short of LSEG consensus estimates of $1.50 a share and $1.99 billion. Skyworks completed its combination with Qorvo in early October, and the first quarter marks the first combined quarter for the two. Super Micro Computer — Shares of the server company jumped 2% after Super Micro earnings per share and revenue beat Wall Street estimates. For fiscal year 2027, the company expects net sales to range between $72 billion and $82 billion, above the LSEG consensus for $69.17 billion. Arista Networks — The cloud networking company gained 4% after current-quarter guidance topped estimates. Arista sees fourth-quarter earnings of $1.26 to $1.30 per share on revenue of $3.9 billion to $4.0 billion. Analysts surveyed by LSEG were looking for $1.15 per share and $3.60 billion. Block — The fintech stock rallied 9% after Block posted third-quarter earnings and revenue that exceeded expectations, and raised guidance for the full year ending December. Adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share topped the $1.03 LSEG consensus estimate, while revenue of $6.72 billion beat the $6.59 billion consensus. Freshworks — The software stock tumbled about 10% even after the customer support ticketing company posted stronger-than-expected third-quarter results and full-year guidance. Freshworks earned an adjusted 22 cents per share on revenue of $245.4 million in the latest quarter, above earnings of 18 cents on revenue of $245.1 million analysts polled by FactSet expected. The stock has recently outperformed, rallying more than 20% over the past three months. — CNBC's Darla Mercado, Deena Zaidi, Paulina Likos, Sarah Min, Davis Giangiulio, Ananya Chetia and Fred Imbert contributed reporting.

headlines.article_text: SpaceX, Tesla stocks fall over 4% on Democrats big win Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Several AI-linked stocks fell as election results came in showing a convincing win by Democrats of both houses of Congress. Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas governor’s race after campaigning for tougher limits on data center development. Investors are weighing whether state-level data center restrictions could delay projects in major buildout markets. In this article CRWV TSLA SPCX NBIS NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT The US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Aaron Schwartz | Bloomberg | Getty Images AI data center stocks came under pressure as Democrats — seen as proponents of moratoriums on the buildout — won big in midterm elections and in key technology hubs like Texas. Markets were already anticipating the Democrats to win the House of Representatives and possibly take Senate control. But the Texas governor mansion going to Democrats was a big blow, analysts said. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who wants to enact an immediate moratorium on data centers in the state, won over incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott. According to Wells Fargo, 27% of planned data center gigawatts is in the Lone Star State. The midterm elections will slow the pace of data center buildouts across the U.S., Dan Ives, partner at Yorkville Ives & Co., said in a note on Wednesday morning. "There is no way to sugarcoat that Democrats taking control especially over the Senate will create some major hurdles for AI and tech legislation in the Beltway over the next 2 years," he said. He added that the election in Texas was the "biggest worry" of the night for tech investors and the AI trade because that's where around 25%-30% of data center gigawatts and capacity will come from. Shares of Elon Musk 's SpaceX shed 7%. The Democrats' victory in Texas is a big setback for Musk , where he heavily backed Republican candidates, and where his companies Tesla and SpaceX are based. Musk spent a record of at least $474 million on the midterms and funneled $224 million into Texas alone, where Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton and Gov. Greg Abbott lost to Democrats. SpaceX is currently building out multiple gigawatts of data center capacity, including projects in Texas. "Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," Musk said in a post on X in the early hours on Wednesday, referring to his speculative plans to build AI infrastructure off-planet. Neoclouds CoreWeave and Iren fell by 7% and 6%, respectively. Peer Nebius Group was down 3% and Oracle shed 4.3%. Nvidia shares were slightly in the red. Tech giants Alphabet , Meta and Microsoft mostly bucked the trend and were higher. The Democratic win in Texas adds to existing pressure on the bull-market-leading AI trade. The Nasdaq-100 index fell into correction territory to end October as concerns mounted that the growth of data center spending by big hyperscalers and private AI juggernauts OpenAI and Anthropic was slowing. "We believe the equity market reaction from the midterms mostly depends on the outcome of the Texas governor's race — a Dem win could potentially be a left-tail event to the AI trade, warned Ohsung Kwon, Wells Fargo's chief equity strategist, in a report this week. Democrats won or retained the governorships in other key data center states Georgia, Pennsylvania and Ohio. Georgia represents 7% of all the planned U.S. datacenter gigawatts, while Ohio and Pennsylvania account for 5% apiece, estimates Wells Fargo. Notable investment strategist Michael Hartnett of Bank of America warned earlier this year that Democrats winning the Senate, combined with taking the Texas governorship could lead to a "big slump" in stocks of more than 10% into year-end. "Data centers went from being a popular economic development tool in 2024 and 2025 to something of a pariah by the time the midterm campaigns gathered steam," wrote the Washington policy team at Optimal Advisory this week. "The midterms are likely to send a message to local and state officials that there is a political upside to blocking, delaying and/or raising the cost of data centers." headlines.article_text: CVS to split off drugstore business Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half of 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would separate CVS's roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. In this article CVS Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT A person walks into a CVS pharmacy near George Washington University in Washington, U.S., August 15, 2024. Kaylee Greenlee Beal | Reuters CVS Health plans to split into two separate public companies by the first half 2028 in what would be one of the largest corporate splits in history, the company announced Wednesday. The move would reverse the company's massive $78 billion acquisition of its insurer, Aetna, and dismantle the vertically integrated healthcare conglomerate it created in 2018. The plan would specifically separate CVS's roughly 9,000 retail pharmacies from its major insurance business and pharmacy benefit manager, Caremark, one of the nation's three largest PBMs. The decision follows a "comprehensive strategic review" by the company's board of directors, according to a news release. It's a stunning reversal for the healthcare powerhouse, which has spent the last two decades working to turn itself into a one-stop health destination. The move also comes as CVS's aggressive turnaround plan under CEO David Joyner shows substantial progress, with the company pursuing $2 billion in cost cuts, store closures, leadership shakeups and efforts to rein in Medicare Advantage costs. "From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination," Joyner said in the release. Shares have jumped roughly 70% since Joyner took the helm in October 2024, bringing the company's market value to $117 billion. The two new companies would both be publicly traded. The insurance and PBM company will retain the CVS Health name and be run by Joyner, while the other company will be called CVS Pharmacy and be led by Prem Shah, who is currently group president of CVS Health. Additional leadership positions and board members will be announced at a later date, CVS said. Existing CVS shareholders will own shares in both companies after the split. The Financial Times on Tuesday first reported the breakup plans. The company's pharmacy business raked in $37.66 billion in 2025 sales, while its insurance unit booked $36.29 billion in revenue and healthcare services segment generated $51.24 billion. On Tuesday, CVS also said it will lump its insurer and PBM with its primary care business Oak Street Health, home-visit provider Signify Health and the company's specialty drug business. CVS also said the split will allow the two companies to experience a "focused strategic agenda" and greater ability to "innovate, adopt technology, increase efficiency," among other benefits. It's not the first time CVS has weighed splitting the company. In October 2024, CVS engaged advisors in a strategic review of its business and considered breaking up its retail pharmacy and insurance units. Even so, Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny said the split "feels like a complete shock" in a Tuesday note. But he said that the retail pharmacy business has been performing well, winning market share from competitors and seeing stabilizing gross margins thanks to CostVantage, a new pharmacy reimbursement model introduced by CVS last year. "In this context, perhaps the outlook for a standalone retail pharmacy (still with meaningful scale and leverage on its own) is stronger now than before," Cherny wrote. He added that "the rationale could also be to avoid what has been relentless state legislative scrutiny over the company's level of vertical integration." The potential breakup also comes as pharmacy benefit managers face mounting bipartisan scrutiny in Washington, D.C., and across states. The company also reported double-digit revenue growth in the U.S. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC the growth is largely due to the company continuing to take market share in what's been a sluggish housing market. In this article W Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Cheng Xin | Getty Images Wayfair on Wednesday said it posted its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic as the furniture retailer continues to win over customers and take market share. The company said it saw double-digit revenue growth in the U.S., reaching about $3 billion, an 11.4% increase from the year prior. Still, international net revenue for the quarter decreased 2.3% year over year to $380 million. The report comes as the housing market remains sluggish. But the furniture and home goods retailer has reported consistent growth over the past year. CFO Kate Gulliver told CNBC that Wayfair's momentum is building as it takes market share. "We see the overall consumer in the U.S. in this category, we think it's roughly flattish, and so that's our [market] share momentum continuing to build," Gulliver said. She added that shopper loyalty, the opening of new stores, the company's luxury furniture business and an emphasis on value has allowed the company to win more consumers. Customers are also continuing to spend, whether at the company's value prices or on the luxury side, she added. "We've been highly promotional for the last few years, and the promotional activity this year is actually very consistent with last year," she said. "It maintains this sort of momentum on promotional activity this year." Here's how the company performed in its third quarter compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG: Earnings per share: 93 cents adjusted vs. 79 cents expected Revenue: $3.42 billion vs. $3.38 billion expected For the period ended Sept. 30, Wayfair reported net income of $62 million, or 45 cents per share, compared with a loss of $99 million, or a loss of 76 cents per share, the year prior. Total revenue grew 9.7% year over year, reaching $3.42 billion. The company said its active customers grew 4.7% year over year, reaching 22.2 million. It also saw a 12.2% increase in orders delivered during the quarter to about 11 million. As the company looks ahead to the holiday season and the fourth quarter, Gulliver said it's maintaining promotional activity similar to last year. She added that the company is confident that its range of prices and products will appeal to a broad base of consumers. "We've seen that growth play out," Gulliver said. "We've seen that flow through to EBITDA, ultimately to net income positive this quarter, which is really another key piece in the story and the momentum here, so we feel very good about the quarter of the performance."
